description:
Soy Catriel Pereira, participante de la sede Cochabamba en el NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. Me interesa la astronomía, los datos abiertos y construir herramientas que cualquiera pueda usar, y por eso elegí el reto Planet X and SPHEREx. 
Mi equipo está construyendo BlinkX: escribes las coordenadas de una zona del cielo y ves un video de cómo cambia en el tiempo con imágenes infrarrojas de SPHEREx, para descubrir astros

Busco integrantes con ganas de aprender y disfrutar el proceso.
summary:
BlinkX is a public web tool that turns NASA SPHEREx infrared images into short time-lapse videos of any patch of sky. Users enter coordinates (right ascension and declination); the tool fetches matching observations across epochs and bands from the mission archive, aligns them, and plays them back so moving objects stand out.

It addresses the Planet X and SPHEREx challenge directly: SPHEREx maps the entire sky every six months in 102 near-infrared bands, producing more data than any astronomer can inspect. 
BlinkX makes that archive explorable by anyone — no downloads, no astronomy background — so volunteers can spot asteroids, comets, browndwarfs, or even a new planet by watching the sky move.
details:
BlinkX is a public web application that turns NASA SPHEREx observations into short time-lapse videos of any region of the sky.

The user enters the coordinates of a sky patch — right ascension and declination — along with a size and an infrared band. The backend queries the mission archive for every observation covering that point across epochs, downloads small cutouts instead of full files, aligns them onto a common grid, renders them to images, and serves the frames back to the browser, which plays them as a looping video with per-epoch dates.

No downloads, no installs, no astronomy background required.

Main Benefit

The main benefit is radical simplification. Working with SPHEREx data normally means handling 60+ MB FITS files, world-coordinate systems, and a 102-channel spectral layout spread across detectors and slew steps.

BlinkX hides all of that behind one form and a play button, while preserving the science — band, epoch, and data-quality flags travel with every frame.

Its intended impact is to widen the volunteer base that hunts moving objects. Since most known comets and brown dwarfs were discovered by volunteers comparing images across time, lowering that task to a single click directly multiplies the chances of new finds, including a possible Planet X.

Technology

We built BlinkX with:

  • Frontend: React, Vite, and Tailwind CSS
  • Backend: Python, FastAPI, Astropy, NumPy, and reproject
  • Infrastructure: Terraform-managed AWS infrastructure using S3 and CloudFront
  • Data sources: NASA/IPAC Infrared Science Archive through its public SIA2 search API and IBE cutout service
  • Mission data: SPHEREx Quick Release hosted on AWS Open Data

Development ran on standard laptops using the AWS free tier — no special hardware required.

Data Pipeline

The application retrieves data live from the NASA/IPAC Infrared Science Archive. Instead of downloading complete FITS files, BlinkX requests small cutouts around the user's selected sky coordinates.

The backend then:

  1. Searches for observations covering the requested region.
  2. Retrieves the relevant cutouts for each epoch.
  3. Processes the astronomical images using Astropy and NumPy.
  4. Reprojects the images onto a common grid.
  5. Renders the processed observations into frames.
  6. Sends the frames to the browser.
  7. Plays them sequentially as a looping time-lapse with the corresponding observation dates.

What Makes BlinkX Creative

What makes BlinkX creative is that it treats time, not spectra, as the discovery dimension.

Instead of showing 102 static channels, it replays the sky itself and lets motion do the talking — the same blink-comparison principle behind Pluto's discovery, rebuilt for the infrared all-sky era.

This approach transforms a complex astronomical data-analysis workflow into an intuitive visual experience that anyone can use.

Engineering Trade-offs

Along the way, the team had to weigh several real-world trade-offs:

  • Cutouts vs. full files: reducing bandwidth and processing requirements.
  • Per-epoch rotation: requiring reprojection before animation.
  • Wavelength differences within a band: maintaining scientific consistency across observations.
  • Silent API truncation limits: ensuring that search results are not unintentionally incomplete.
  • Free-tier-only infrastructure: keeping the entire system within a strict budget.

BlinkX combines astronomical data processing, cloud infrastructure, and an intuitive visual interface to make SPHEREx observations dramatically easier to explore — turning a complex archive into something as simple as choosing a patch of sky and pressing play.
